title: 富士登山「安全」「親しみ」両立模索…弾丸登山は抑制も親子連れ減少で子ども料金設定へ
extracted_text:
昨年初めて全面的な登山規制を実施した富士山で、７月の開山を前に今季の登山の事前登録が始まった。静岡、山梨両県は入山料・通行料の徴収など規制の枠組みを維持する一方、静岡県側で子ども向け料金の設定に向けた調査を行ったり一部ルートで開山日を早めたりし、「安全で親しみやすい山」へ模索を続けている。（静岡支局　大坪祐市、富士吉田通信部　涌井統矢）
「今シーズンも世界文化遺産・富士山の保全と登山者の安全確保のため登山規制を実施します。ご理解とご協力をお願いします」。静岡県の鈴木康友知事は４月２７日の記者会見で呼びかけた。山梨県は同日から登山客の事前登録を開始。静岡県は５月８日から始める。
同県は昨年、公式アプリによる事前登録を導入。〈１〉入山料４０００円の納付〈２〉登山ルールの事前学習〈３〉午後２時～翌午前３時に入山する際の山小屋予約――を義務づけた。夜通し登る弾丸登山は激減し、県警によると、開山期（７～９月）の遭難者は前年比２８人減の３６人、死者・行方不明者は６人減の０人になった。
一足先に２０２４年から登山規制を導入した山梨県も昨年、２０００円だった通行料を倍の４０００円にするなど足並みをそろえた。弾丸登山はほぼなくなり、夜に山小屋の前で防寒シートや寝袋にくるまって仮眠をとる登山者の姿も見られなくなったという。
一方、一部で「富士山離れ」も顕著になった。静岡県側の御殿場ルートでは登山者が前年比で半減。トレイルランの練習で頻繁に登っていた愛好家が入山料を敬遠したとみられている。
県や山小屋関係者の総括では「親子連れが減った」との指摘もあった。親子４人で登ると入山料は１回で計１万６０００円。家族連れの予約が１、２件にとどまった山小屋もあったという。そのため、子どもの入山料を学校行事以外でも減免する制度の導入に向け、県は今年、入山者の年齢調査を行う。
また山梨側で７月１日、静岡側で同１０日と例年異なっている開山日についても、静岡県は初めて３ルートのうち須走ルートを同１日に前倒しする。頂上近くで山梨側の吉田ルートと合流しており、開山日を合わせることで富士登山者の６割を占める吉田ルートの混雑を緩和するほか、閉山中の須走ルートに人が迷い込むのを避けるねらいがある。
同ルート５合目にある東富士山荘の米山千晴代表（７５）は、開山日のずれがなくなることで「急な雷や強風の際も須走側の山小屋で登山者を受け入れる対応ができる」と話す。
立教大の西川亮准教授（観光政策）は「持続可能な観光にしていくためには、リピーターや若者が登りたくなるような動機付けが求められる。子どもに親しみやすさを持ってもらうため料金負担を減らす措置は合理的だ」と話している。
（詳しくはこちら）
translated_text:
Pre-registration for this season's Mount Fuji climbing has begun ahead of the July opening, marking the first year of full climbing regulation implementation. Both Shizuoka and Yamanashi prefectures are maintaining their regulatory framework including mountain entry and通行料 fees. Meanwhile, Shizuoka is conducting research on child-focused pricing and has moved up the opening date for some routes, continuing its push to make the mountain 'safe and approachable.'

'We will implement climbing regulations again this season to preserve the World Cultural Heritage site of Mount Fuji and ensure climber safety. Your understanding and cooperation are requested.' Shizuoka Governor Yasutomo Suzuki stated at an April 27 press conference. Yamanashi Prefecture began climber pre-registration on the same day, with Shizuoka starting on May 8.

Shizuoka introduced pre-registration via an official app last year, requiring three things: payment of a 4,000 yen mountain entry fee, pre-study of climbing rules, and mountain hut reservations for those entering between 2 PM and 3 AM. Overnight 'bullet climbing' has drastically decreased, with distress incidents during the opening season (July-September) down by 28 from the previous year to 36, and deaths or missing persons reduced by 6 to zero.

Yamanashi Prefecture, which introduced climbing regulations ahead of schedule in 2024, also aligned its approach last year by doubling the通行料 from 2,000 to 4,000 yen. Bullet climbing has virtually disappeared, and the sight of climbers sleeping wrapped in thermal sheets and sleeping bags in front of mountain huts at night is no longer seen.

However, a 'Mount Fuji disengagement' has become noticeable in some areas. On Shizuoka's Gotemba route, climber numbers halved compared to the previous year. Hobbyists who frequently climbed for trail running training are believed to be avoiding the entry fees.

Some summarizing by prefectural officials and mountain hut operators noted a 'decline in families.' For a family of four climbing together, entry fees total 16,000 yen per person. Some mountain huts had only one or two family reservations. In response, the prefecture will conduct an age survey of climbers this year to establish a system for reducing or waiving children's entry fees beyond school events.

Additionally, regarding the opening dates, which have traditionally differed between July 1 in Yamanashi and July 10 in Shizuoka, Shizuoka has for the first time moved up the Subashiri route opening to the same date among its three routes. It converges with Yamanashi's Yoshida route near the summit, and aligning the opening dates aims to ease congestion on the Yoshida route, which accounts for 60% of Mount Fuji climbers, as well as prevent people from entering the closed Subashiri route.

Representing the East Fuji Mountain Lodge at the 5th station, 75-year-old Chihiro Yoneyama said that with the opening dates aligned, 'we can accept climbers at Subashiri-route mountain huts even in cases of sudden thunderstorms or strong winds.'

Ryo Nishikawa, Associate Professor of Tourism Policy at Rikkyo University, noted: 'To make tourism sustainable, motivation is needed for repeat visitors and young people to want to climb. Reducing the fee burden for children to make the mountain more approachable is a reasonable measure.'
title_en: Mount Fuji Climbing Seeks Balance Between Safety and Accessibility; Bullet Climbing Curbed But Family Visits Decline Leads to Child Pricing
